title: MATLAB tutorial: matrices, vectorization, functions and plotting — cv.cm
description: Learn MATLAB basics (and free GNU Octave): run scripts, create vectors and matrices, index them, use loops, functions, anonymous functions, errors and plots.
answer: MATLAB is a numerical computing language and environment from MathWorks in which every value is a matrix. You write `A * B` for a matrix product, `A .* B` for element-wise multiplication, index from 1, and replace many loops with vectorized expressions. It includes plotting and a large set of toolboxes for engineering and science. GNU Octave is a free, open-source alternative that runs most basic MATLAB code unchanged.

sections.h: What MATLAB is and who uses it
body: MATLAB ("matrix laboratory") began as a tool by Cleve Moler for easy access to linear algebra libraries and became a commercial product of MathWorks. It combines a language, an interactive desktop, plotting, and toolboxes for signal processing, control systems, optimization, statistics, image processing and machine learning. Simulink, a companion product, models dynamic systems with block diagrams.

MATLAB is widely used in engineering and science courses, research labs, and industries such as automotive, aerospace and finance. It requires a paid license (many universities provide one). GNU Octave is free software with largely compatible syntax; it covers the core language and many functions but not MathWorks toolboxes or Simulink.

Install MATLAB from MathWorks, use MATLAB Online in a browser, or install GNU Octave from octave.org (Windows, macOS, Linux). Code is saved in `.m` files. A script is a file of commands; you run it by typing its name, without `.m`, in the Command Window.

body.code:
matlab -batch "hello"   # MATLAB from a terminal
octave hello.m          # GNU Octave
# Hello, world!

body: Comments start with `%`. A line that ends without a semicolon prints its result, so `x = 5` shows `x = 5`, while `x = 5;` stays silent.
Variables are created by assignment and need no declaration. Numbers are `double` (64-bit floating point) by default, and even a single number is a 1-by-1 matrix.

body: Square brackets build arrays: spaces or commas separate columns, semicolons separate rows. Indexing uses parentheses and starts at 1; `end` means the last index and `:` means "all".

body.code:
v = [3 1 4 1 5];
v(1)               % 3
v(end)             % 5
v(2:4)             % [1 4 1]
v * 2              % [6 2 8 2 10]
v(v > 2)           % [3 4 5]   logical indexing
A = [1 2; 3 4];
A(2, :)            % second row: [3 4]
A'                 % transpose:  [1 3; 2 4]
A * A              % matrix product: [7 10; 15 22]
A .* A             % element-wise:   [1 4; 9 16]
b = [5; 11];
x = A \ b          % solves A*x = b: [1; 2]
z = zeros(2, 3);   % also ones, eye, rand
r = 0:0.25:1;      % [0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1]

body: Operators with a dot (`.*`, `./`, `.^`) work element by element; without the dot they follow the rules of linear algebra. The backslash operator solves linear systems and is more accurate than computing `inv(A) * b`.

body.code:
score = 85;
if score >= 90
    disp('A')
elseif score >= 80
    disp('B')
else
    disp('C')
end

total = 0;
for k = 1:10
    total = total + k;
end
fprintf('total = %d\n', total)   % total = 55

n = 3;
while n > 0
    n = n - 1;
end

switch 'red'
    case {'red', 'green'}
        disp('a color')
    otherwise
        disp('unknown')
end

body: Every block ends with `end`. Many loops can be replaced by a vectorized expression: the loop above is the same as `sum(1:10)`, which is shorter and usually faster. If you must build an array in a loop, preallocate it first, for example `result = zeros(1, 1000);`.

A function lives in its own file whose name matches the function name. A function can return several outputs. Scripts can also contain local functions at the end of the file in recent MATLAB versions.

body.code:
[m, s] = stats([2 4 4 5 7])   % m = 4.4000, s = 1.8166
[biggest, where] = max([3 9 2])   % biggest = 9, where = 2

f = @(x) x.^2 + 1;            % anonymous function
f(3)                          % 10
f([1 2 3])                    % [2 5 10]
fzero(@(x) x.^2 - 2, 1)       % 1.4142, a root near 1
integral(f, 0, 1)             % 1.3333

body: Anonymous functions, created with `@`, are often passed to other functions such as `fzero`, `integral`, `arrayfun` or optimization routines. Write them with element-wise operators (`.^`) so they also work on vectors.
MATLAB also has a `table` type for column-oriented data with named variables, similar to a spreadsheet; `readtable` loads CSV and Excel files into it.

Raise an error with `error`, optionally with an identifier such as `'demo:negative'`, and handle it with `try ... catch`. The caught object (an `MException` in MATLAB) has `identifier` and `message` fields.

body.code:
try
    safe_sqrt(-4);
catch err
    fprintf('%s: %s\n', err.identifier, err.message)
end
% demo:negative: Input must be non-negative, got -4

body: Use `warning(...)` for problems that should not stop the program. Without the check, `sqrt(-4)` would not fail at all: it returns the complex number `0 + 2i`.

sections.h: A small complete program: analyze and plot data

body.code:
% temps.m - analyze a week of temperatures
temps = [21.5 23.0 19.8 25.1 24.3 18.9 22.7];
days = 1:numel(temps);

avg = mean(temps);
[hottest, idx] = max(temps);
above = days(temps > avg);

fprintf('Average: %.2f\n', avg)
fprintf('Hottest: %.1f on day %d\n', hottest, idx)
fprintf('Days above average: %s\n', mat2str(above))

plot(days, temps, '-o')
hold on
plot(days, avg * ones(size(days)), '--')
xlabel('Day'); ylabel('Temperature (C)')
title('Temperatures this week')
legend('Daily', 'Average')
% Average: 22.19
% Hottest: 25.1 on day 4
% Days above average: [2 4 5 7]

body: The script uses logical indexing to find the days above the average without a loop, then draws a line chart with markers and a dashed average line. The same code runs in GNU Octave.

body.note: Common beginner mistakes: using `*` or `^` where you meant element-wise `.*` or `.^` (you get a dimension error or a matrix power); indexing with 0 (`v(0)` is an error); forgetting semicolons, which floods the output; naming a script or variable like a built-in function (`sum`, `max`, `i`), which hides the function; using `i` and `j` as loop variables when complex numbers are involved; and growing arrays inside loops instead of preallocating.

The GNU Octave manual if you use Octave, including its notes on MATLAB compatibility.
Learn vectorization, `readtable` for data files and the plotting functions next.

faq.q: Is there a free version of MATLAB?
faq.a: MATLAB itself needs a license, although MathWorks offers trials and many universities provide campus licenses. GNU Octave is a free, open-source program that runs most basic MATLAB code.

faq.q: What is the difference between * and .* in MATLAB?
faq.a: `*` is matrix multiplication from linear algebra, which requires matching inner dimensions. `.*` multiplies corresponding elements of two arrays of the same size.

faq.q: Is GNU Octave fully compatible with MATLAB?
faq.a: Not fully. Core syntax, matrices, functions and plotting are largely compatible, but Octave lacks MathWorks toolboxes, Simulink and some newer MATLAB features, and it accepts a few extra syntax forms of its own.

faq.q: Why does MATLAB start indexing at 1?
faq.a: MATLAB follows mathematical notation, where the first element of a vector or matrix is element 1. Fortran, R and Julia use the same convention.

faq.q: Should I learn MATLAB or Python?
faq.a: Learn MATLAB if your course, lab or company uses it, especially with Simulink or specific toolboxes. Python with NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib is free and more general-purpose, and the concepts transfer between the two.
